Life after death?

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
....meet the world's leading researcher on life after death

Unique Selling Point:
A question that affects all of humanity is: is there life after death? In this insert we explore what scientists say about this.

Summary:
A few years ago the first major study of life after death was concluded under Dr Sam Parnia. While at University of Southampton, Parnia was the principal investigator of the AWARE Study, This study which concluded in 2012 included 33 investigators across 15 medical centers in the UK, Austria and the USA and tested consciousness, memories and awareness during cardiac arrest. The accuracy of claims of visual and auditory awareness was examined using specific tests. One such test consisted in installing shelves, bearing a variety of images and facing the ceiling, hence not visible by hospital staff, in rooms where cardiac-arrest patients were more likely to occur. The results of the study were published in October 2014; both the launch and the study results were widely discussed in the media. In this insert we talk to Sam Parnai about this study, the results and life after death.

Further information:
A few years ago the first major study of life after death was concluded under Dr Sam Parnia. While at University of Southampton, Parnia was the principal investigator of the AWARE Study, This study which concluded in 2012 included 33 investigators across 15 medical centers in the UK, Austria and the USA and tested consciousness, memories and awareness during cardiac arrest. The accuracy of claims of visual and auditory awareness was examined using specific tests. One such test consisted in installing shelves, bearing a variety of images and facing the ceiling, hence not visible by hospital staff, in rooms where cardiac-arrest patients were more likely to occur. The results of the study were published in October 2014; both the launch and the study results were widely discussed in the media. In this insert we talk to Sam Parnai about this study, the results and life after death.

Parnia is known for his involvement and research in the field of emergency medicine and cardiac arrest resuscitation. He conducts research on, and advocates for wider application of, best practices for resuscitation when people die; namely better, perhaps automated cardiopulmonary resuscitation techniques, the use of targeted temperature management, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, brain oximetry, and prevention of reperfusion injury, and wrote his book, Reversing Death (published in the UK as the Lazarus Effect) as part of that effort. He says that many people who are actually dead from heart attacks or blood loss could be resuscitated up to 24 hours after their decease if contemporary best practices as defined by the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation were used promptly.
The main focus of Parnia's research has been in the optimization of brain monitoring and oxygen delivery methods with a goal of reducing long-term brain injuries as well as disorders of consciousness such as a persistent vegetative state.[14] In order to avoid these disabilities, Parnia believes the study of consciousness should be a routine part of cardiac arrest brain injury research.[15] The other side of his work, which he conducts with a team at the State University of New York and across multiple other medical centers in the UK, is consciousness during cardiac arrest. This includes near-death experiences.

Consciousness and near death experience research

Parnia has advocated for the use of the term "actual death experience" instead of near death experience (NDE), to describe human experiences that occur during a period of cardiac arrest. He has stated: “contrary to perception, death is not a specific moment but a potentially reversible process that occurs after any severe illness or accident causes the heart, lungs and brain to cease functioning. If attempts are made to reverse this process, it is referred to as ‘cardiac arrest’; however, if these attempts do not succeed it is called ‘death’. He has mostly studied those who have no heart beat and no detectable brain activity for periods of time and believes cardiac arrest is the optimal model to help understand the human experience of death.
In 2001, Parnia and colleagues published the results of a year-long study of cardiac arrest survivors. 63 survivors were interviewed; 7 had memories of the time they were unconscious and 4 had experiences that, according to the study criteria, were NDEs. Out of body claims were tested by placing figures on suspended boards facing the ceiling, not visible from the floor. No conclusions could be drawn due to the small number of subjects.

The AWARE I study concluded in 2014. A review article analysing the results reports that, out of 2060 cardiac arrest events, only 101 of 140 cardiac arrest survivors could complete the questionnaires. Of these 101 patients only 9% could be classified as near death experiences. 2 more patients (2% of those completing the questionnaires) described "seeing and hearing actual events related to the period of cardiac arrest". These two patients' cardiac arrests did not occur in areas equipped with ceiling shelves hence no images could be used to objectively test for visual awareness claims. One of the two patients was too sick and the accuracy of her recount could not be verified. For the second patient instead, it was possible to verify the accuracy of the experience and to show that awareness occurred paradoxically some minutes after the heart stopped, at a time when "the brain ordinarily stops functioning and cortical activity becomes isoelectric." The experience was not compatible with an illusion, imaginary event or hallucination since visual (other than of ceiling shelves' images) and auditory awareness could be corroborated.

Aware II study
As of May 2016, a posting at the UK Clinical Trials Gateway website describes plans for AWARE II, a two-year multi-center observational study of 900-1500 patients experiencing cardiac arrest, with subjects being recruited as Aug 1 2014 and a trial end date of May 31, 2017.

Brain/mind hypotheses
Parnia and others have suggested that a mind that is mediated by, but not produced by, the brain, is a possible way to explain NDE.

Press Release:


Is there life after death? Can our spirits live on, long after our bodies die? These questions have plagued mankind for centuries, but following a
comprehensive medical study, US researchers believe they could soon unlock the answer. Carte Blanche explores consciousness and the “near death”
experience.

Script:


Sam Parnia:
Death is not a philosophical point. Death has s a science and as we understand is that it can be reversed even after it has taken place.
V/O:
Dr Sam Parnia of Stony Brook University on Long Island in the US is one of the world’s leading researchers in the field of emergency medicine and cardiac arrest resuscitation.
Link 1:
As resuscitation specialist he daily encounters people who have died.
V/O:
And in the resuscitation room he and his team fight to bring these people back to life. Remarkably, some of those who are brought back, recall strange experiences while they were dead.
Sam:
And what we are finding is that people are providing eye witness testimonies of what it is like for all of us when we cross over that threshold of death.
V/O:
These people are describing what is commonly known as Near Death Experiences or NDE’s.

David and Hillary White of Honeydew experienced something akin to an NDE a few years ago.
David:
I had an office at home with three steps, three tall steps down. And I slipped on the steps and I landed on my back and I could not move.
Link 2:
David was in excruciating pain and paramedics rushed him to hospital where he was X-rayed and given very strong morphine-based pain killers. A few hours later Hillary drove him home
Hillary:
And I noticed him starting to go very quiet. He had been talking and then started to go very quiet. And then I could not wake him up. I was maybe five hundred meters from home, got into the drive. And I was looking at him, he had gone grey. He had not gone white, he'd gone a very funny colour.

Dave:
All I can remember is that I could see a white wall coming towards me. And then I heard my father's voice saying: "Not yet David, it is too early. Go back. Go back.

Hillary:
And so as I parked the car I went around to pick him up, to try and shake him. My phone rang. One of the guys at the office phoned me to say: "How is your husband doing?" And it is at that point that he actually woke up.
V/O:
David’s story is typical of what people with near death experiences report to medical staff.
Link 3:
Sam himself has come across these types of claims many times after a resuscitation. It intrigued him.
V/O:
More so because it seems that it is a universal human experience.
Sam:
People by and large have very similar experiences when they die irrespective of background. Whether they are an atheist, whether they have... let's say they are Christian, of Islamic background, Judaism, Hinduism or Buddism etc. The core of the experience that people have is very similar. They describe feeling immensel peaceful. They describe a sensation where they are being drawn away. They describe a sensation of meeting deceased relatives. They often describe seeing a being that is full of love, compassion that they describe as being perfect, that guides them through their experience. And what is really fascinating is that they then themselves start to review everything that they had done and said in their lives.
V/O:
The phenomenon of NDE’s also seems to become more frequent as advances in modern resuscitation techniques have started to alter what we traditionally thought death to be.
Sam:
After that moment, there is still a period of time in which we can bring a person back. But they are dead. It is not that they are half alive, they are dead. What we have to understand is that the cells do not decompose the moment someone dies. There is a period where the brain does not work, the organs don't function but the cells are gradually decomposing. So when that decomposition of cells reaches a point that we can never bring a person back, nobody knows. It could be hours, days, it looks like it could be at least twenty hours. We do not really know how long it is.
Link 4:
This means that we should look at death as a process and not a singular event.
Sam:
You could say to me that if your brought them back to life then they clearly were not dead. And the answer is that is not correct. As a scientist and intensive care doctor we study people who have objectively died, because we know what happens to the brain when people have died what happens to all the vital organs when people have died. There is a whole science around that. So in essence I study people who have objectively gone through a period of death. And therefore what they recall at that time I describe as an actual death experience. It is not near death it is what actually occurred beyond death, what happens after death.
V/O:
To establish that their patients are really dead, Sam and his team monitor events second by second and record when the heart has stopped and the brain has ceased functioning.
Sam
For most people we cannot bring them back, but for fifteen to twenty percent we do bring them back. And they ar the ones that tell us what it was like to go beyond that point the first hour, the first two hour, three hours of death.
Link 5:
For Sam this suggested that consciousness seems to survive bodily death.
Sam:
And therefore I decided to study a small group of people who have gone through cardiac arrest to see if they had any memories or recollections. And it was a small study, but what was interesting was that we have found that approximately ten percent of people had memory recollections that were compatible with what people were describing in the past as a so called near death experience.
V/O:
This was a bold move because the study of these experiences is by many researchers not considered a subject for serious scientific consideration. Some even call it pseudo-science. Further, these experiences have traditionally been dismissed by the medical fraternity as the result of chemical activity in the brain of dying people. However, Sam contends that NDE’s can and should be studied scientifically.
Sam:
Millions of people have gone through cardiac arrest all over the world. Small children to adults who have come back and have recalled these types of experiences. So, anybody with a neutral mind would have to be open to these. You can't’ dismiss something that is occurring all over the world and just say “I don’t agree with it, I don’t believe in it.”
Link 6:
Then Sam initiated major scientific study. I was called the Aware Study.
Sam:
We as part of the AWARE study which was a multi-national, large study, looking at awareness and people's experiences during cardiac arrest involved more than 15 medical centres both in Europe and the United States. And we recruited more than two thousand subjects, the largest ever study of this phenomenon. ….who were brought back, who had gone through death and had been revived. Unfortunately, because of current practice, most of those people could not be revived. We had about a hundred forty odd patients who were brought back.
V/O:
To find objective scientifically verifiable data they followed an interesting protocol in all the resuscitation rooms.
Sam:
We have developed systems where we had images that were placed in the resuscitation areas that are either visible for a person who looks from down above. So there is an image above there heads but they can see if they open their eyes. Because it is possible, although very unlikely that some people may open their eyes. We never see that but we have to include that as a possibility.

The other is that you talk to the people and they say: "You know what Doctor I was at the ceiling." So the only way that we can test this, to say that it was correct or not in a theoretical level is to have an additional image that is only visible from the ceiling down. That is different.

And on top of that they come back and tell us conversations that have occurred so we have to have auditory stimuli that we could use.

So our current model, aside from monitoring the brain, we provide visual stimuli that are visible from different angles in the room as well as auditory stimuli to test whether they truly had consciousness preserved. I think the key thing to understand is; does consciousness continue when a person has gone through death and their brain has shut down. And that is what we are trying to test irrespective of what we call it.
Link 7:
The results of the 4-yearlong study were published in December 2014.
Sam:
The results of the AWARE study were positive. We had cases of people who had awareness that we could corroborate and we could demonstrate for the first time that there appear to be conscious of awareness going on for at least three to five minutes after the period when a person had died and when their brain would have appeared to have stopped functioning and they were able to recall precise details that we could corroborate independently.
V/O:
They also found that some patients recall more than others. David for example had only partial recall, but both he and Hillary are convinced that he had actually died as a reaction to the strong medication.
David:
I believe I passed away……..
Sam:
So what we believe this is, is there is an iceberg model of consciousness. At the tip of that iceberg you have the two or three percent who have full awareness, full consciousness even though they have gone through death. Slightly below that you have people who have lost some of their memory but can remember scattered parts of it. And underneath the surface are the eighty, ninety percent who do not have any explicit recall but most likely they also had some awareness present. They just can't recall it. And that is what has lead us to our new study where we are trying to delve in deeper.
Link 8:
Sam’s ground-breaking research will in future help us to understand consciousness and the brain better, but it is also important on another level.
Sam:
Whether we like it or not that question is going to affect every single one of us one day. And for sure, when I face that moment I think I would like to know what is going to happen to me. It is the biggest mystery and it is the biggest point that everyone worries about. So to just ignore it and not conduct scientific studies I think is a betrayal of our current abilities today.

Sam: We as part of the AWARE study which was a multi-national, large study, looking at awareness and people's experiences during cardiac arrest involved more than 15 medical centres both in Europe and the United States. And we recruited more than two thousand subjects, the largest ever study of this phenomenon. ….who were brought back, who had gone through death and had been revived. Unfortunately, because of current practice, most of those people could not be revived. We had about a hundred forty odd patients who were brought back. V/O: To find objective scientifically verifiable data they followed an interesting protocol in all the resuscitation rooms. Sam: We have developed systems where we had images that were placed in the resuscitation areas that are either visible for a person who looks from down above. So there is an image above there heads but they can see if they open their eyes. Because it is possible, although very unlikely that some people may open their eyes. We never see that but we have to include that as a possibility. The other is that you talk to the people and they say: "You know what Doctor I was at the ceiling." So the only way that we can test this, to say that it was correct or not in a theoretical level is to have an additional image that is only visible from the ceiling down. That is different. And on top of that they come back and tell us conversations that have occurred so we have to have auditory stimuli that we could use. So our current model, aside from monitoring the brain, we provide visual stimuli that are visible from different angles in the room as well as auditory stimuli to test whether they truly had consciousness preserved. I think the key thing to understand is; does consciousness continue when a person has gone through death and their brain has shut down. And that is what we are trying to test irrespective of what we call it. Link 7: The results of the 4-yearlong study were published in December 2014. Sam: The results of the AWARE study were positive. We had cases of people who had awareness that we could corroborate and we could demonstrate for the first time that there appear to be conscious of awareness going on for at least three to five minutes after the period when a person had died and when their brain would have appeared to have stopped functioning and they were able to recall precise details that we could corroborate independently. V/O: They also found that some patients recall more than others. David for example had only partial recall, but both he and Hillary are convinced that he had actually died as a reaction to the strong medication. David: I believe I passed away…….. Sam: So what we believe this is, is there is an iceberg model of consciousness. At the tip of that iceberg you have the two or three percent who have full awareness, full consciousness even though they have gone through death. Slightly below that you have people who have lost some of their memory but can remember scattered parts of it. And underneath the surface are the eighty, ninety percent who do not have any explicit recall but most likely they also had some awareness present. They just can't recall it. And that is what has lead us to our new study where we are trying to delve in deeper. Link 8: Sam’s ground-breaking research will in future help us to understand consciousness and the brain better, but it is also important on another level. Sam: Whether we like it or not that question is going to affect every single one of us one day. And for sure, when I face that moment I think I would like to know what is going to happen to me. It is the biggest mystery and it is the biggest point that everyone worries about. So to just ignore it and not conduct scientific studies I think is a betrayal of our current abilities today.

metadata.Further information: A few years ago the first major study of life after death was concluded under Dr Sam Parnia. While at University of Southampton, Parnia was the principal investigator of the AWARE Study, This study which concluded in 2012 included 33 investigators across 15 medical centers in the UK, Austria and the USA and tested consciousness, memories and awareness during cardiac arrest. The accuracy of claims of visual and auditory awareness was examined using specific tests. One such test consisted in installing shelves, bearing a variety of images and facing the ceiling, hence not visible by hospital staff, in rooms where cardiac-arrest patients were more likely to occur. The results of the study were published in October 2014; both the launch and the study results were widely discussed in the media. In this insert we talk to Sam Parnai about this study, the results and life after death. Parnia is known for his involvement and research in the field of emergency medicine and cardiac arrest resuscitation. He conducts research on, and advocates for wider application of, best practices for resuscitation when people die; namely better, perhaps automated cardiopulmonary resuscitation techniques, the use of targeted temperature management, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, brain oximetry, and prevention of reperfusion injury, and wrote his book, Reversing Death (published in the UK as the Lazarus Effect) as part of that effort. He says that many people who are actually dead from heart attacks or blood loss could be resuscitated up to 24 hours after their decease if contemporary best practices as defined by the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation were used promptly. The main focus of Parnia's research has been in the optimization of brain monitoring and oxygen delivery methods with a goal of reducing long-term brain injuries as well as disorders of consciousness such as a persistent vegetative state.[14] In order to avoid these disabilities, Parnia believes the study of consciousness should be a routine part of cardiac arrest brain injury research.[15] The other side of his work, which he conducts with a team at the State University of New York and across multiple other medical centers in the UK, is consciousness during cardiac arrest. This includes near-death experiences. Consciousness and near death experience research Parnia has advocated for the use of the term "actual death experience" instead of near death experience (NDE), to describe human experiences that occur during a period of cardiac arrest. He has stated: “contrary to perception, death is not a specific moment but a potentially reversible process that occurs after any severe illness or accident causes the heart, lungs and brain to cease functioning. If attempts are made to reverse this process, it is referred to as ‘cardiac arrest’; however, if these attempts do not succeed it is called ‘death’. He has mostly studied those who have no heart beat and no detectable brain activity for periods of time and believes cardiac arrest is the optimal model to help understand the human experience of death. In 2001, Parnia and colleagues published the results of a year-long study of cardiac arrest survivors. 63 survivors were interviewed; 7 had memories of the time they were unconscious and 4 had experiences that, according to the study criteria, were NDEs. Out of body claims were tested by placing figures on suspended boards facing the ceiling, not visible from the floor. No conclusions could be drawn due to the small number of subjects. The AWARE I study concluded in 2014. A review article analysing the results reports that, out of 2060 cardiac arrest events, only 101 of 140 cardiac arrest survivors could complete the questionnaires. Of these 101 patients only 9% could be classified as near death experiences. 2 more patients (2% of those completing the questionnaires) described "seeing and hearing actual events related to the period of cardiac arrest". These two patients' cardiac arrests did not occur in areas equipped with ceiling shelves hence no images could be used to objectively test for visual awareness claims. One of the two patients was too sick and the accuracy of her recount could not be verified. For the second patient instead, it was possible to verify the accuracy of the experience and to show that awareness occurred paradoxically some minutes after the heart stopped, at a time when "the brain ordinarily stops functioning and cortical activity becomes isoelectric." The experience was not compatible with an illusion, imaginary event or hallucination since visual (other than of ceiling shelves' images) and auditory awareness could be corroborated. Aware II study As of May 2016, a posting at the UK Clinical Trials Gateway website describes plans for AWARE II, a two-year multi-center observational study of 900-1500 patients experiencing cardiac arrest, with subjects being recruited as Aug 1 2014 and a trial end date of May 31, 2017. Brain/mind hypotheses Parnia and others have suggested that a mind that is mediated by, but not produced by, the brain, is a possible way to explain NDE.
